title: The Sicker Patients

scenario.situation: A post-launch review shows patients prescribed the new drug Velorin have a 30-day readmission rate nearly double that of untreated patients.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The medical director fears Velorin is causing harm and wants to suspend prescribing pending a safety review.
scenario.question: Is Velorin actually hurting patients, or is something else explaining the outcome gap?

decisions.prompt: The medical director wants a fast answer. How do you frame the investigation?

options.label: Adverse-event audit on Velorin patients
options.detail: Pull all reported adverse events and readmissions for patients who received Velorin.
options.consequence: You find a long list of complications in Velorin patients — but you have no comparator. You've only described the treated group without asking who they were before treatment started.
options.divergenceCost: Anchored on the safety hypothesis and ignored the baseline composition of the treated group.

options.label: Diagnostic segmentation by baseline severity
options.detail: Compare patient characteristics — disease severity, comorbidities — between treated and untreated groups before looking at outcomes.
options.consequence: You immediately see the treated and untreated groups are not alike: Velorin patients entered care far sicker. The outcome gap now has a candidate explanation that has nothing to do with the drug's safety profile.

options.label: Time-series of readmissions since launch
options.detail: Plot system-wide readmission rates month by month and mark the Velorin launch date.
options.consequence: Readmissions did tick up after launch — but Velorin was introduced at the same time as a winter respiratory surge. The temporal correlation is completely confounded.
options.divergenceCost: Used a before/after design that conflated the drug launch with an unrelated seasonal trend.

options.label: Survey prescribing physicians
options.detail: Ask physicians why they chose Velorin for certain patients.
options.consequence: Physicians say they prescribe it for 'complex cases' — useful context, but qualitative and slow. It doesn't quantify the severity gap or rule out harm with the data already on hand.
options.divergenceCost: Chose a slow qualitative instrument when the severity signal was already in the structured patient records.

decisions.prompt: Segmenting by severity reveals the groups differ. Which metric do you use to fairly compare outcomes?

artifact.title: 30-day readmission rate — Velorin vs. untreated (unadjusted)
artifact.caption: Raw readmission rates look damning for Velorin — but treated patients were systematically sicker at baseline. Are we comparing like with like?

options.label: Raw 30-day readmission rate by treatment group
options.detail: Compare unadjusted readmission rates between Velorin and untreated patients.
options.consequence: The treated group still looks far worse — but you now know they were sicker going in. Reading the raw rate as a drug effect is like blaming the ICU for high mortality. You're measuring case mix, not treatment impact.
options.divergenceCost: Compared outcomes across groups with fundamentally different baseline risk — the difference is confounded by indication.

options.label: Severity-adjusted readmission rate (within matched severity tiers)
options.detail: Stratify patients into severity tiers and compare readmission rates within each tier between treated and untreated patients.
options.consequence: Within every severity tier, Velorin patients actually readmit at a lower rate than untreated patients of the same severity. The drug appears beneficial once you control for who received it.

artifact.title: 30-day readmission rate by severity tier — Velorin vs. untreated
artifact.caption: Within every severity tier, Velorin patients readmit less. The drug was being prescribed to the sickest patients — their worse raw outcomes reflected their disease, not the drug.

decisions.prompt: After severity adjustment, Velorin is associated with lower readmissions in every tier. What do you tell the medical director?

options.label: "Velorin is beneficial — the safety concern is unfounded, keep prescribing as-is."
options.detail: Declare the drug safe and effective based on the adjusted analysis.
options.consequence: You've cleared the drug on observational data that still can't rule out unmeasured confounders — other severity proxies you didn't capture may still be driving the residual gap. Acting on this without flagging the limitation risks a false sense of certainty.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed a causal benefit from a severity-adjusted observational study — unmeasured confounders remain.

options.label: "The raw signal is explained by confounding by indication — adjusted, Velorin looks beneficial, but we need a quasi-experiment or prospective controlled comparison before changing policy."
options.detail: Present the finding, name the confounding mechanism, and recommend a causal confirmation step.
options.consequence: You've defused a premature suspension decision with evidence, named exactly why the raw comparison was misleading, and handed the team a concrete next step — a propensity-matched cohort study or an instrumental variable analysis — to nail down the causal effect.

insight: Velorin looked harmful only because physicians rationally prescribed it to the sickest patients — a textbook case of confounding by indication. Once outcomes were compared within severity tiers, the drug showed a consistent protective association in every stratum. The lesson is that when treatment assignment is driven by the very factor that predicts bad outcomes, raw comparisons are structurally biased; you must adjust for baseline severity, match on propensity, or use a quasi-experimental design before any safety or efficacy claim holds.
